        FROM ubuntu:20.04

        # Config
        ENV TZ=America/Los_Angeles
        RUN ln -snf /usr/share/zoneinfo/$TZ /etc/localtime && echo $TZ > /etc/timezone

        # Install dependencies

        # System setup
        RUN apt update
        RUN apt install -y sudo build-essential python3 python3-pip virtualenvwrapper git wget curl screen postgresql

        ## Node.js
        RUN curl -sL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_14.x | sudo -E bash -
        RUN apt-get install -y nodejs
        RUN npm install -g yarn
        RUN npm install -g typescript

        ## pip
        RUN pip3 install --upgrade git-review
        RUN pip3 install nodeenv
        RUN nodeenv -n 14.7.0 /root/.node/14.7.0/

        # Entrypoint
        RUN echo "#!/bin/sh \n\
        echo "fs.inotify.max_user_watches before update" \n\
        cat /etc/sysctl.conf | grep fs.inotify \n\
        echo "______________________________________________updating inotify ____________________________________" \n\
        echo fs.inotify.max_user_watches=524288 | tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf && sysctl -p \n\
        echo "updated value is" \n\
        cat /etc/sysctl.conf | grep fs.inotify \n\
        exec bash \
        " >> /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh
        RUN chmod +x /usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh
        RUN ln -s `which pip3` /usr/bin/pip

        # Secrets config
        ADD secrets.json /root/.plasmic/

        # Expose server port
        EXPOSE 3003

        ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh"]

I am a cfp reviewer for the common ground track at Bsides Las Vegas; below are the instructions I was given. I would like for you to do your best to review talks that have gone through BSides Common ground talk already by reading through the archives and create a guide of what you think makes a good common ground talk. Also, create a guide of what I should look for in a submission. From that, please create a rubric of responses that I can use when I am reading through the abstracts. Assume I'm going to spend a 1:30 on each; I will spend 1:00 reading their abstract and :30 revising the templated rubric response. So having many sample rubric responses that I can revise given various different submission acceptance or rejection scenarios would be extremely helpful. 

        Hey there, BSides!


        You’re currently one of the folks we hope to have help us make this year happen as part of the 2025 BSides Las Vegas Program Committee.

        Accept/Decline

        We understand people get busy, or have major life events suddenly thrust upon them during interesting times.  If for some reason you’re unable to participate this year, please let us know so we can seek alternative awesomeness to fill your particular pair of pointy shoes.  

        Planned Dates:

        Proving Ground Open:  2/10

        All Other Tracks Open:  3/3

        All Tracks (including PG) Close.  Reviews Start:  4/7

        PG Acceptance/Pairings Announced:  4/21

        All Reviews Due:  4/28

        Track Selections Complete:  5/9

        Initial Acceptance & Decline Letters Sent:  5/12

        Confirmations Complete:  6/2

        BSides Las Vegas Conference:  Monday 8/4, Tuesday 8/5, and Wednesday 8/6


        Yes, you read that right.  This year BSides Las Vegas will be three days.  Well, 2.5.  We’re doing a full day on Monday, a full day on Tuesday, and a half day on Wednesday.  


        Based on the conversations I’ve had with the BSides board and the Operations folks so far, our masking policy will also be revised this year.  We will NOT be requiring masks in the general conference areas, unless something major changes before the conference (Bird Flu, anyone?).  We WILL still require masks in the separate Skytalks space over in the Platinum.  


        These masking updates are not officially released on the web site yet, but I’m hoping to get them carved in stone before we open the general CFP next month.


        Review Process:

        Team Access:

        Pretalx is located here: https://pretalx.com/orga/event/security-bsides-las-vegas-2025/

        New Members: you will receive an invitation via e-mail to join Pretalx, our conference platform.  Please accept it, and update your login credentials.

        Returning Members: your account should be active with your previous login.  If you need help that the password reset can’t provide, please contact me directly.

        After we have everyone's responses/accounts in place, we will offer a couple of live kick-off sessions before the review period starts for anyone who wants to learn about Pretalx, the conference, or how we do reviews. 
        Submission:  Authors submit proposals.  Track chairs will review the queue weekly, swap proposals between tracks as necessary, and notify authors if submitted proposals are incomplete/blatantly inadequate.

        Review:  Once we close the CFP, you will have a set of proposals to review.  Please provide thoughtful and constructive feedback for each submission, focusing on originality, quality, and relevance to the track theme and the state of the security industry.  Your score and comments help us pick the best talks, and also help authors improve.

        The “What do you think?” field is released to authors after the conference schedule is published.  Please use it.  We want declined proposals to have actionable and polite constructive feedback.  If you feel a talk was missing something, this is your opportunity to help the submitter get better at submitting.  

        Comments in the  “Internal Comments for Review Committee” field are for the program committee only, and are never released.

        This year, we’ve added a required “Outline” field.  Hopefully this will drive more authors to contribute a detailed outline like our example submissions.

        Selection: Track and Program Chairs build a balanced, comprehensive program for each track and for the conference as a whole.  We rely heavily on your scores and comments, and may also reach out to authors for clarification/modification of their proposals, or to other experts with relevant knowledge to help make final determinations.

        Acceptance: Acceptance (and decline) emails are sent based on the track and program chair selections.  Clear accepts and clear declines go out immediately, and we work our way from the top and bottom of the stack to the middle, until we have a full slate of presenters and a small pool of alternates who can cover for talks that have to drop out.

        Feedback: Public reviewer comments are released for all submissions.  


        Attending: 

        You’re part of this committee because you’re awesome, so COME TO THE CONFERENCE.  Reviewers who attend get a staff badge (which has special access to the breakfast and lunch buffets, and events like the staff party and speaker reception).  Come to Vegas and hang out with each other and our speakers so we can all grow together.

        If you have questions reach out to cfp@bsideslv.org, or hit me up directly via @daemontamer on the BSides LV Slack, X, Bluesky, Mastodon (daemontamer@infosec.exchange) or however else you personally typically get hold of me.

        Lastly, Dr. Russ Handorf has graciously agreed to pitch in as a program chair this year so that we can continue to have nice things at BSLV.  He’s russ.handorf@bsideslv.org and we’ll get him added to Slack channels and Google groups as we clean them up.

        Sincerely,
        Daemon Tamer

        Guide to Using REPO_STRUCTURE.md
        1. Purpose
        The REPO_STRUCTURE.md file is an auto-generated, definitive map of our monorepo's file and directory structure. Its primary purpose is to serve as a single source of truth for the layout of the project at any given time.
        This document is not meant to be edited manually. It is updated automatically by running the pnpm docs:structure command, which ensures it always reflects the current state of the repository.

        2. How We Use It
        This file is a critical tool for both the human developer and the AI assistant, ensuring that both have a shared, accurate understanding of the project's structure.

        For the Human Developer
        Quick Reference: Use this file as a quick way to understand where different parts of the project are located without having to manually expand directories in your file explorer.
        Onboarding: It's an invaluable tool for new team members to quickly get a high-level overview of the entire codebase.
        For the AI Assistant (A Critical Workflow Step)
        This is the most important use case for this file in our collaborative workflow.

        The Problem: During development, especially during refactoring, the file system changes frequently. The AI assistant's internal "memory" of the file structure can quickly become outdated, leading it to try and move or access files that are no longer there, which causes errors.
        The Solution: We will use REPO_STRUCTURE.md to synchronize the AI's understanding with the project's reality.
        Before prompting the AI to perform any file system operations (like mv, rm, mkdir, or creating a new file in a specific location), you should first ensure the REPO_STRUCTURE.md file is up-to-date by running pnpm docs:structure.
        Then, you will explicitly instruct the AI to read this file as part of your prompt.
        Example Prompts for the AI:
        "First, please read the REPO_STRUCTURE.md file to get the current layout of the project. Once you have done that, please run the command to move the src directory into apps/main-app/."
        "Please review the REPO_STRUCTURE.md file. Based on the current structure, create a new file named colors.ts inside the packages/design-system/tokens directory."
        By following this process, we ensure that the AI's actions are always based on the ground truth of the repository, which significantly reduces errors and streamlines our development process.

        3. How to Create and Update the File
        The REPO_STRUCTURE.md file is generated by a script in our root package.json.

        Prerequisites
        You must have the tree command-line utility installed in your development environment. This is handled by our project's dev.nix file.
        Command
        To create or update the file, run the following command from the root of the monorepo:

        pnpm docs:structure
        This command executes the tree utility, ignoring specified directories (like node_modules and .next), and saves the output to the REPO_STRUCTURE.md file, overwriting its previous content. It is best practice to run this command after making any significant changes to the project's file or directory structure.
